newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau heads into last polls before China takeover.
newsitem.headline: Macau heads into last polls before China takeover.

text.p: Candidates offering karaoke and dim sum parties are jostling for votes as election fever heats up in Portuguese-run Macau for the last polls before Lisbon hands its Asian pearl back to China.

Only eight of the Legislative Assembly's 23 seats are up for direct election in Sunday's poll. The remainder of the assembly, which will straddle the handover to China on December 20, 1999, are either indirectly elected or appointed by the governor.

Campaigners in gaudy uniform teeshirts and sashes were out wooing the voters, and popular entertainers from Hong Kong have been enlisted to appear on the racy election posters or on television campaign adverts to promote the candidates.

Backers have been knocking on doors offering free karaoke parties and inviting voters to Chinese "dim sum" lunch parties catering to up to 1,000 diners per sitting, all in a bid to woo that vital ballot on Sunday, Macau residents said on Tuesday.

Macau has been ruled from Portugal for almost five centuries and, like nearby Hong Kong, it is set to become an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China under Beijing's scheme for reunifying lost Chinese territories.
Macau, best known for its casinos, has regularly hit the headlines recently for a spate of gangland bombings, but the two-week election campaign has proceeded smoothly so far.

The electoral system is only partly democratic. The 116,000 voters directly elect eight members of the assembly, while eight are indirectly elected by business, labour and community associations and seven are appointed by the governor.
In Hong Kong, politicians battle over relations with China, human rights, democracy and the future of their legislature.
But Macau campaigning is over bread-and-butter issues such as crime, jobs and the war against red tape, political analysts in the territory said.
In stark contrast with Hong Kong, which reverts to China two and a half years earlier next July 1, Macau's assembly is not fighting for its own survival beyond the 1999 handover.
China plans to dismantle Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council and appoint a new "provisional legislature", which has sparked cries of foul play from democrats and from Britain.
But Beijing has given Macau's election process a nod of approval and allowed a "through-train" assembly.

"Macau has respected China's views, and consulted China on its electoral reforms of the past 20 years, but Britain exceeded the bounds of its agreements with China on the question of the pace of democratisation," a Chinese official in Macau said.
Macau's electors vote for lists of candidates, casting a ballot for the group of their choice, not for an individual.
The contestants are not called "parties". They are interest groups who team up before the polls, held every four years.

A record 62 candidates on the 12 lists are vying for the eight direct seats. They range from well-established pro-Beijing labour and neighbourhood associations to representatives of the employees working in Hong Kong tycoon Stanley Ho's casino empire as well as pro-democracy and liberal groups.
Two ethnic lists represent people originating from China's Fujian Province and the Portuguese-speaking Eurasian "Macanese".
In the previous election four years ago, two staunchly pro-China lists won 49 per cent of the vote and four seats.

The other four were won by four lists from pro-democracy, liberal and independent business and civil service groups. The indirect poll takes place on the same day with a result that is already clear. Just one candidate is contesting each seat.
